target.rawSql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT generate_series(
           LEAST(
             (now() AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date - interval '2 years',
             COALESCE(
               (SELECT to_timestamp(min(bucket_start)) AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'
                FROM cex_prices),
               (now() AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date
             )
           ),
           (now() AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date + interval '14 days',
           interval '1 day'
         ) AS d
)
SELECT
  (d + interval '17 hours') AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York' AS "time",
  (d + interval '2 days 17 hours') AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York' AS "timeEnd",
  'FX market closed' AS text
FROM days
WHERE EXTRACT(DOW FROM d) = 5
ORDER BY 1

description: Raw collected series first, then the regime analytics derived from them. Read it top-down: is there data for this venue and product, what does the store hold across every venue, what does the data say about volatility by hour, and how does this currency's whole pair set compare. The candlestick and the vol panel read one product at a time; the cross-pair index deliberately reads the whole currency at once. Every panel except Spot ticks reads the candle tier, so Venue source lists candle venues only; the tick-only venues (kraken among them) are under Tick venue and drawn by the Spot ticks panel at the bottom.

links.title: All data
links.tooltip: Widen the time range to start at this series' own first collected bar, keeping the current venue and product. Exists because the time picker has no such preset — its presets are all relative to now, and none of them can know when collection actually started, so any of them wide enough to hold the whole series also pads the chart with dead space. Drag-selecting on a chart zooms in and there is no equally obvious way back out, so this is the way back out.

links.title: Last 24h
links.tooltip: Narrow to the last day, keeping the current venue and product. At 60s buckets this is the widest window where individual candles are still readable.

panels.description: The raw collected candles for the selected venue and product, straight off the store with no derivation. Shows the full open/high/low/close rather than the close alone, because the range within each bucket is most of what a candle records and plotting only the close discards it. This is the panel to check first: if it is empty, nothing below it means anything. A sparse series with visible gaps is not a fault — a venue emits no candle for a bucket with no trades, so a thinly traded book genuinely looks like scattered marks rather than a continuous run. Over a long window at a small bucket size the candles compress into a solid band; narrow the time range to read individual bars.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT
  to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS "time",
  "open",
  "high",
  "low",
  "close",
  "volume"
FROM cex_prices
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
  AND source = ${venue_source:sqlstring}
  AND product_id = ${venue_product:sqlstring}
  AND granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
ORDER BY bucket_start

panels.title: Price — ${venue_product} on ${venue_source} (${granularity}s candles)

panels.description:
Which sources cover which products in the candle tier, how much history each holds, and how fresh each is. The store-inventory definition for both dashboards.

Every (source, product, bucket width) the store has EVER held is a row, so a series that stopped entirely stays visible instead of dropping out of a window. Read three columns together: Bars (all time) is how much history exists, Buckets in window is whether it is still arriving, and Age (buckets) is how late it is. All-time bars with zero in-window buckets is a series that STOPPED — the one reading no windowed panel can give you.

AGE IS COUNTED IN BUCKETS, NOT SECONDS, and that is why the buckets column is the colored one. A daily series is 86400 seconds old just before its next bar lands, so an absolute bound tuned for 60s bars marks a perfectly healthy daily reference red forever. Dividing by the series' own bucket width makes one bound correct for both: about 1 is current, 2 is the bar in progress, orange at 4 and red at 8. Age in seconds is kept beside it as raw context and is deliberately not colored.

The window is independent of the dashboard time range on purpose: what is arriving now should not change when you pan back to look at history.

targets.rawSql:
-- The candle tier's store inventory and its freshness in one definition,
-- absorbing what the old Last candle age tile and the FX dashboard's What is
-- in the store table each answered on their own.
--
-- DRIVEN FROM ALL TIME, windowed only in a column. A series that stopped
-- entirely has no rows inside any window, so a windowed GROUP BY drops it and
-- the reader cannot tell "stopped" from "never configured" -- that reading is
-- what the FX table contributed and it has to survive the merge. Here every
-- (source, product, bucket width) the store has ever held is a row, and
-- buckets_in_window falling to 0 is what says it stopped.
--
-- STALENESS IS CADENCE-RELATIVE, which is why age_secs is not the colored
-- column. A daily series is 86400 seconds old the moment before its next
-- bucket lands, so any absolute bound correct for 60s bars paints a healthy
-- daily reference permanently red -- the defect that made the FX table's
-- 300/3600 thresholds wrong rather than merely noisy, measured on a source
-- whose bars are 86400s wide. age_cadences divides by the series' own bucket
-- width, so one number reads correctly for both: about 1 is current, 2 is the
-- bucket in progress, and the colored bounds sit at 4 and 8 so a weekend of a
-- daily reference does not read like an outage.
WITH lifetime AS (
  SELECT
    c.source,
    c.product_id,
    c.granularity_secs,
    count(*) AS bars_all_time,
    max(c.bucket_start) AS last_bucket
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
),

windowed AS (
  SELECT
    c.source,
    c.product_id,
    c.granularity_secs,
    count(*) AS buckets
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  WHERE c.bucket_start
    >= extract(epoch FROM now()) - (${coverage_mins:sqlstring}::bigint * 60)
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)

SELECT
  l.source,
  l.product_id,
  l.granularity_secs,
  l.bars_all_time,
  coalesce(w.buckets, 0) AS buckets_in_window,
  to_timestamp(l.last_bucket) AS latest_bucket,
  (extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_bucket)::bigint AS age_secs,
  round(
    (extract(epoch FROM now()) - l.last_bucket) / l.granularity_secs, 1
  ) AS age_cadences
FROM lifetime AS l
LEFT JOIN windowed AS w
  ON
    l.source = w.source
    AND l.product_id = w.product_id
    AND l.granularity_secs = w.granularity_secs
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3

panels.title: Candle coverage (all time, window ${coverage_mins} min)

panels.description:
What is this pair's realized volatility by hour of day, and is each hour a measurement or an artefact. Bars are the standard deviation of log-returns per bucket, in basis points; the darker series is the largest single move in that hour.

READ THE SAMPLE SIZE, on the right axis. A standard deviation over four returns and one over four hundred draw identical bars, so an hour that is merely thinly collected otherwise reads as a real volatility regime. Return pairs is the honest denominator — returns that survived the adjacent-bucket guard — and the raw bar count rides along in the tooltip. This is what the Weekend vs weekday table was for, and it is now attached to the reading it qualifies rather than sitting two panels away.

THE ADJACENT-BUCKET GUARD is why these numbers can be trusted at all. A return is computed only when the previous bar is exactly one bucket earlier, so a gap in collection never yields a return spanning it. Without it, an overnight or weekend gap produces one enormous return attributed to whichever hour the gap ended in — a convincing and entirely false time-of-day effect, in exactly the hours a reader most wants to understand.

ONLY IN-SESSION BARS ARE READ. A bar counts only when it falls inside an open span of the FX session fence, so post-close and weekend bars never enter an hour's population, on every venue alike, a 24/7 crypto venue included, because the reading this feeds is the weekday quoting posture. The fence is imposed from the calendar rather than inferred from the bars: a grid vendor prints a moving bar every minute of the weekend, so nothing in the series itself marks those bars as out of session. Hours are in the selected timezone; the session boundaries are New York time regardless.

targets.rawSql:
-- Realized vol by hour of day, in session only, with its own sample size
-- beside it -- absorbing the Weekend vs weekday table, whose remaining job was
-- exactly that sample size for this panel.
--
-- THE ADJACENT-BUCKET GUARD IS LOAD-BEARING, not defensive style. A return is
-- computed only when the previous bar is exactly one bucket earlier, so a gap
-- in collection never produces a return spanning it. Without the guard an
-- overnight or weekend gap yields one enormous "return" attributed to whatever
-- hour the gap happened to end in, which fabricates a convincing and entirely
-- false time-of-day effect -- and the hours a collector is most likely to have
-- gaps in are exactly the hours a reader is most interested in.
--
-- SAMPLE SIZE RIDES ALONGSIDE for the same reason: a standard deviation over
-- four returns and one over four hundred render as identical bars, so an hour
-- that is merely thinly collected reads as a real vol regime. return_pairs is
-- the honest denominator -- the number of returns that survived the guard --
-- and bars is the raw count it came from.
--
-- ONLY IN-SESSION BARS ARE READ, and the session is imposed, not inferred.
-- fx_session_window (migration 0015) is the session authority: a bar enters
-- only when its bucket start falls inside a span reading 'open'. Read the span
-- half-open (starts_at <= t < ends_at) -- BETWEEN would admit a bar stamped
-- at the Friday close itself, because the closed span starts on that same
-- instant. A bar with no covering span is dropped as well, so outside the
-- view's horizon the panel goes empty rather than silently reading unfenced.
--
-- This is what the weekday/weekend split's removal was waiting for. The split
-- was ratified away because it decided nothing under a weekday-only posture
-- while halving every hour's sample, but removing it without a fence POOLED
-- the out-of-session bars into the same per-hour populations rather than
-- dropping them: a grid vendor was measured printing 28.6% of its series out
-- of session with 99% of those bars moving, concentrated in the hours around
-- the Friday close and the Sunday open. The fence applies to every venue
-- alike, a 24/7 crypto venue included -- the reading this panel feeds is the
-- weekday quoting posture, so a crypto weekend is as far outside the
-- population as an FX vendor's indicative one.
--
-- FENCE BEFORE THE RETURNS, never after. Filtering the bars first leaves the
-- last bar before the close and the first after the reopen two days apart,
-- so the adjacent-bucket guard refuses the return that would span the
-- weekend. Fencing the returns instead would be wrong, not merely redundant:
-- on a grid vendor the bar before the Sunday reopen is an out-of-session
-- print exactly one bucket earlier, so the guard would pass that return and
-- admit it at every reopen.
--
-- DO NOT REACH FOR `volume` AS THE DISCRIMINATOR, which is the obvious guess
-- and is wrong. Measured across 14 days: every one of that vendor's 20,162 bars
-- carries zero volume, in session and out alike, so the column identifies the
-- VENDOR as indicative and never a BAR as out-of-session. What does discriminate
-- is grid-versus-tape -- an indicative vendor emits a bar every minute with no
-- intraday gaps and identical counts across pairs, while a real tape's counts
-- differ per pair because a minute with no tick produces no bar at all. This
-- panel needs neither: the fence above imposes the session instead.
WITH open_spans AS (
  -- Narrowed to the spans overlapping the window first, so the per-bar test
  -- below scans a handful of rows rather than the view's whole horizon.
  SELECT
    s.starts_at,
    s.ends_at
  FROM fx_session_window AS s
  WHERE
    s.state = 'open'
    -- <= because the bar filter below is inclusive at the window's top edge:
    -- a bar stamped at the window's end on a reopen instant is still in it.
    AND s.starts_at <= $__timeTo()
    AND s.ends_at > $__timeFrom()
),

bars AS (
  SELECT
    c.bucket_start,
    c.close
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(c.bucket_start)
    AND c.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring}
    AND c.product_id = ${venue_product:sqlstring}
    AND c.granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
    AND EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM open_spans AS o
      WHERE
        o.starts_at <= to_timestamp(c.bucket_start)
        AND to_timestamp(c.bucket_start) < o.ends_at
    )
),

returns AS (
  SELECT
    to_timestamp(b.bucket_start) AS bucket_ts,
    CASE
      WHEN
        lag(b.bucket_start) OVER w
        = b.bucket_start - nullif(${granularity:sqlstring}, '')::bigint
        AND lag(b.close) OVER w > 0
        AND b.close > 0
        THEN ln(b.close / lag(b.close) OVER w)
    END AS r
  FROM bars AS b
  WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY b.bucket_start)
),

hourly AS (
  SELECT
    extract(HOUR FROM r.bucket_ts AT TIME ZONE ${hour_tz:sqlstring})::int
      AS hour_of_day,
    r.r
  FROM returns AS r
)

SELECT
  lpad(h.hour_of_day::text, 2, '0') AS hour,
  stddev_samp(h.r) * 10000 AS vol_bps,
  max(abs(h.r)) * 10000 AS max_abs_move_bps,
  count(h.r) AS return_pairs,
  count(*) AS bars
FROM hourly AS h
GROUP BY h.hour_of_day
ORDER BY h.hour_of_day

panels.title: Realized vol by hour (${hour_tz})

panels.description:
Of every pair carrying this currency, which moved most and when. Each is indexed to 100 at its first bar inside the visible window, which is what makes them comparable: raw closes are not — EUR-USD sits near 1.08 while EUR-JPY sits near 170 — so an overlay of them is one flat line and one off-scale line. The base is the first bar in the WINDOW rather than the series' first bar ever, so panning or zooming re-bases every series and the comparison always describes the period you are looking at.

QUIET PAIRS ARE NAMED RATHER THAN DROPPED. The pair list is every registered pair for this currency on this venue; one with no bar in the window appears in the legend marked "registered, no bars in window" and draws no line. It used to filter through a liveness view that drops the source, so a pair this venue carries but had not printed lately left the picker entirely — meaning this panel, which is the one discharging the per-symbol acceptance condition, showed FEWER pairs the wider an outage got.

Scoped to one venue, matching the rest of this dashboard: two vendors carrying the same pair would draw two nearly identical lines and double the legend for no information.

targets.rawSql:
-- Cross-pair overlay, indexed to 100 at each series' first bar INSIDE the
-- window. Absolute levels are not comparable across pairs -- EUR-USD sits
-- near 1.08 while EUR-JPY sits near 170 -- so an overlay of raw closes is one
-- flat line and one off-scale line, and "which moved most" has no readable
-- answer. Indexing puts every pair on a common percent axis.
--
-- The base is the first bar in the WINDOW, not the series' first bar ever, so
-- panning or zooming re-bases every series and the comparison stays about the
-- period actually on screen.
--
-- QUIET PAIRS ARE NAMED, NOT DROPPED, which is the whole redesign. The pair
-- list used to run through a liveness view that drops the source, so a pair
-- this venue carries but has not printed lately simply left the picker -- and
-- this panel discharges the per-symbol acceptance condition, which means it
-- showed FEWER pairs as an outage widened. The list is now every registered
-- pair for the currency on this venue, and a pair with no bar in the window
-- gets a labelled legend entry with no line instead of vanishing. An earlier
-- version argued against emitting those rows on the grounds that a NULL series
-- reads as broken; that was correct while absence meant "this venue does not
-- carry it", and is wrong now that absence means "registered and quiet", which
-- is a reading worth having.
WITH selected AS (
  SELECT s.product_id
  FROM unnest(ARRAY[${pairs:sqlstring}]::text[]) AS s (product_id)
),

bars AS (
  SELECT
    c.product_id,
    c.bucket_start,
    c.close
  FROM cex_prices AS c
  WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(c.bucket_start)
    AND c.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring}
    AND c.product_id = ANY (ARRAY[${pairs:sqlstring}]::text[])
    AND c.granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
),

base AS (
  -- The earliest bar each pair has in the window, which is its index base.
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (b.product_id)
    b.product_id,
    b.close
  FROM bars AS b
  ORDER BY b.product_id, b.bucket_start
),

quiet AS (
  -- The registry check is what makes the legend's "registered" claim TRUE. The
  -- selected set is the raw picker expansion, and registry membership is
  -- enforced only upstream in the pairs variable -- so a stale multi-selection
  -- carried across a venue switch, or a value adopted from a URL, would
  -- otherwise get a row asserting this venue carries a pair it does not. Before
  -- the labelled arm existed such a value produced silently nothing; turning
  -- that into a positive claim is what makes the check necessary rather than
  -- decorative.
  SELECT s.product_id
  FROM selected AS s
  WHERE
    EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM instrument_registry AS r
      WHERE
        r.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring}
        AND r.product_id = s.product_id
    )
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM bars AS b WHERE b.product_id = s.product_id
    )
)

SELECT
  to_timestamp(b.bucket_start) AS "time",
  b.product_id AS metric,
  -- nullif guards a zero base. Without it one bad series divides by zero and
  -- fails the whole panel rather than just itself.
  100.0 * b.close / nullif(f.close, 0) AS value
FROM bars AS b
INNER JOIN base AS f ON f.product_id = b.product_id
UNION ALL
SELECT
  to_timestamp($__unixEpochFrom()) AS "time",
  q.product_id || ' (registered, no bars in window)' AS metric,
  NULL AS value
FROM quiet AS q
ORDER BY 1, 2

panels.title: Cross-pair index — ${currency} pairs on ${venue_source} (first bar = 100)

panels.description:
The tick-tier venues, which no panel above can show. kraken, erapi, frankfurter, pyth and orca (the Orca Whirlpool pool price, product TGBP-USDC) write only spot ticks, so they never appear in the Venue source picker — that picker and every panel driven by it read the candle tier. coinbase writes both, so its ticker appears here as well as its candles above. This panel is where those venues are represented on this page: pick a product with Tick product and every selected Tick venue that printed it inside the window draws one line, so a peg or a reference rate reads across venues at once. A venue that has printed the product but not in the window draws nothing; widen the window or check Tick coverage on the market-data dashboard.

GAPS UNDER FIVE MINUTES ARE JOINED, longer ones are not. With more than one venue selected, two venues rarely print in the same second, so below their poll cadence most aligned rows are half empty and an unjoined line would draw almost nothing; joining gaps up to five minutes closes that. A longer gap breaks the line only where another selected venue printed in the missing bucket. A bucket NO selected venue printed has no row at all and is drawn straight across, so do not read an unbroken line here as proof of no outage; Tick coverage on the market-data dashboard is the panel for that. The once-a-day reference venues are drawn as points where the panel's point density allows.

AVERAGED INTO THE PANEL'S INTERVAL. The default window is thirty days and the minute-cadence venues print tens of thousands of ticks across it, so each line is the mean price per display interval rather than every print. Zoom in until the interval falls below a venue's poll cadence to see its raw prints; Price by source on the market-data dashboard plots them unaggregated.

Not scoped by Currency or Venue source, deliberately: both are scoped to the candle venue's registry, so coupling this panel to them would hide exactly the tick-only products it exists to show.

targets.rawSql:
-- The tick tier, one line per venue for one product. Every other panel on
-- this dashboard reads cex_prices, so a venue that only writes spot_ticks
-- (kraken, erapi, frankfurter, pyth, orca) is invisible to them; this is
-- where those venues are represented on the page. coinbase writes both tiers.
--
-- AVERAGED PER DISPLAY INTERVAL because the default window is thirty days and
-- a minute-cadence venue prints tens of thousands of ticks across it. The
-- column is bare inside both macros: Grafana captures a macro argument with a
-- regex that stops at the first closing paren, so a to_timestamp(...) inside
-- one truncates the argument. The group alias emits epoch seconds, which the
-- time_series format reads as time directly.
SELECT
  $__unixEpochGroupAlias(observed_at, $__interval),
  source AS metric,
  avg(price) AS value
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(observed_at)
  AND source = ANY (ARRAY[${tick_source:sqlstring}]::text[])
  AND product_id = ${tick_product:sqlstring}
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2

panels.title: Spot ticks — ${tick_product} by tick venue

panels.description:
Where the market puts tGBP, from both of its venues on one axis: the Orca Whirlpool pool spot (spot_ticks, source orca) and the Coinbase TGBP-USDC candle close (cex_prices, the finest granularity Coinbase has stored for the product). A gap between the two lines is a disagreement between the pool and the exchange; the estimator's fair, which composes from GBP/USD and the observed basis, is the panel below.

Fixed to TGBP-USDC and to these two sources, deliberately: no template variable drives this row, so the pickers above can be anywhere and this row still answers the one question it exists for.

NO DATA IS A READING, NOT A FAULT. On a keyless or paused stack the Orca collector writes no rows and the Coinbase collector may not carry the product, and an empty line here says exactly that. Check Tick coverage on the market-data dashboard before reading an empty panel as a broken one.

The Orca line is averaged into the panel's interval and joins gaps under five minutes, the same treatment as Spot ticks above; the Coinbase close is drawn one point per candle.

targets.rawSql:
-- The Orca pool leg. orca is a tick-only venue, so it writes spot_ticks and
-- never cex_prices; averaged per display interval, as Spot ticks is.
SELECT
  $__unixEpochGroupAlias(observed_at, $__interval),
  'orca spot' AS metric,
  avg(price) AS value
FROM spot_ticks
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(observed_at)
  AND source = 'orca'
  AND product_id = 'TGBP-USDC'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2

-- The Coinbase leg, the candle close at the finest granularity stored for
-- the product, so the line does not depend on the Granularity picker.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(bucket_start) AS "time",
  "close" AS "coinbase close"
FROM cex_prices
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(bucket_start)
  AND source = 'coinbase'
  AND product_id = 'TGBP-USDC'
  AND granularity_secs = (
    SELECT min(granularity_secs)
    FROM cex_prices
    WHERE source = 'coinbase'
      AND product_id = 'TGBP-USDC'
  )
ORDER BY bucket_start

panels.title: tGBP market — Orca pool spot and Coinbase close

panels.description:
What the fair-value estimator published for TGBP-USDC (fair_price): the fair, in USDC per tGBP on the left axis, and the smoothed basis on the right. Read it against the panel above: fair is the center the estimator holds, the two lines above are where the market trades.

A BREAK IN THE FAIR LINE IS A PAUSE OR A SILENT ESTIMATOR. fair is NULL exactly when the regime is paused, and never drawn as zero; a stretch with no rows at all means the estimator was not publishing. Gaps under five minutes are joined, so a short pause can read as a straight segment; the regime timeline below is the panel that shows it.

The basis is set only in an FX-anchored regime, so it drops out whenever the anchor below leaves fx. Both series are averaged into the panel's interval.

NO DATA on a keyless or paused stack is the correct reading: the estimator publishes nothing for a pair it has no legs for.

targets.rawSql:
-- The estimator's output for the pair. avg ignores NULL, so a bucket that
-- is paused throughout stays NULL rather than collapsing to zero.
SELECT
  $__unixEpochGroupAlias(ts, $__interval),
  avg(fair) AS fair,
  avg(basis) AS basis
FROM fair_price
WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
  AND product_id = 'TGBP-USDC'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

panels.title: tGBP estimator — fair and basis

panels.description:
Which regime the estimator composed TGBP-USDC under, and which leg anchored the mid, over time (fair_price). A degraded regime shows its degrade beside it (degraded: <which>), so every state the estimator writes is drawn as written; a state this panel has no color for draws in blue under its own name rather than being hidden.

Only the changes are drawn: each band starts at the first tick that entered the state, and the last tick in the window closes the final band. A stretch where the estimator wrote nothing is NOT shown as a gap here; the fair line above breaks there.

NO DATA on a keyless or paused stack is the correct reading: the estimator publishes nothing for a pair it has no legs for.

targets.rawSql:
-- Change points only: a thirty-day window at the estimator's tick cadence
-- is far more rows than a state timeline needs. The regime is read as
-- written, with any degrade appended, so a new regime or degrade value draws
-- under its own name with no edit here. The window filter sits inside the
-- subquery so the first tick in the window always opens a band, and the
-- last tick is kept so the final band ends where the data does.
SELECT
  to_timestamp(ts) AS "time",
  regime AS "regime",
  anchor AS "anchor"
FROM (
  SELECT
    ts,
    CASE WHEN degrade IS NULL THEN regime
      ELSE regime || ': ' || degrade END AS regime,
    anchor,
    lag(regime) OVER w AS prev_regime,
    lag(degrade) OVER w AS prev_degrade,
    lag(anchor) OVER w AS prev_anchor,
    lead(ts) OVER w AS next_ts
  FROM fair_price
  WHERE $__unixEpochFilter(ts)
    AND product_id = 'TGBP-USDC'
  WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY ts)
) AS t
WHERE prev_anchor IS NULL
  OR next_ts IS NULL
  OR anchor <> prev_anchor
  OR regime <> CASE WHEN prev_degrade IS NULL THEN prev_regime
    ELSE prev_regime || ': ' || prev_degrade END
ORDER BY ts

panels.title: tGBP estimator — regime and anchor

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM cex_prices ORDER BY 1
list.description: The venue whose collected series is being shown. Single-select: the candlestick and the vol panel each read one venue and product at a time, and the cross-pair index reads one venue across many pairs, so two vendors carrying the same pair never draw duplicate lines. CANDLE VENUES ONLY: this lists the sources in the candle tier, so a venue that writes only spot ticks (kraken, erapi, frankfurter, pyth) is absent by construction, not by omission. Those are under Tick venue, which drives the Spot ticks panel at the bottom; coinbase writes both tiers, so it appears in both pickers.
list.label: Venue source
list.name: venue_source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM cex_prices ORDER BY 1

list.definition:
SELECT DISTINCT legs.c
FROM (
  SELECT i.product_id, i.base AS c FROM instruments i
  UNION ALL
  SELECT i.product_id, i.quote FROM instruments i
) legs
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM instrument_registry r
  WHERE r.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring}
    AND r.product_id = legs.product_id
)
ORDER BY 1
list.description: The currency umbrella: pick one and both the Venue product and the Pairs pickers below offer only pairs with that currency on either leg. This is the selector the dashboard was built without, and the README recorded that selecting by currency needed products tagged by currency family, which was a schema change rather than a dashboard one. That schema landed as the instruments dimension, so this reads the dimension's base and quote legs rather than splitting the product id, which means EURC and EUR are known to be the stablecoin and the fiat of the same currency instead of two unrelated strings. Scoped to the selected venue, for the same reason the Venue product picker is: an unfiltered list invites choosing a currency this venue does not quote, which renders nothing and reads as a broken panel.
list.label: Currency
list.name: currency
list.query:
SELECT DISTINCT legs.c
FROM (
  SELECT i.product_id, i.base AS c FROM instruments i
  UNION ALL
  SELECT i.product_id, i.quote FROM instruments i
) legs
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM instrument_registry r
  WHERE r.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring}
    AND r.product_id = legs.product_id
)
ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT c.product_id FROM cex_prices AS c JOIN instruments AS i ON i.product_id = c.product_id WHERE c.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND ${currency:sqlstring} IN (i.base, i.quote) ORDER BY 1
list.description: The product to show, listing only what the selected venue actually carries AND only pairs with the selected Currency on either leg. Both filters are load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Without the source filter the list offers every product any source has ever written, inviting a symbol the chosen venue does not and could not quote. Without the currency filter the candle panels and the cross-pair index could be pointed at unrelated currencies at once (AUDD-USDC beside EURC pairs), which is a selection that describes nothing. Listed from the candle tier, unlike Currency and Pairs, which read the registry: a currency this venue only ticks leaves this list empty, which is the honest signal that there are no candles to draw. The committed default is TGBP-USDC, the basis pair of the market planned as the first on mainnet. Its tape is thin, so a sparse candle panel on the default is the venue rather than a fault; EURC-USDC has the densest traded tape and is the one to verify against when checking that a panel renders.
list.label: Venue product
list.name: venue_product
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT c.product_id FROM cex_prices AS c JOIN instruments AS i ON i.product_id = c.product_id WHERE c.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND ${currency:sqlstring} IN (i.base, i.quote) ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT granularity_secs FROM cex_prices WHERE source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND product_id = ${venue_product:sqlstring} ORDER BY 1
list.description: Bucket size, in seconds, listing only the values the selected venue and product actually hold. Query-driven rather than a fixed list, and the change is a bug fix: the fixed list offered every bucket size the schema permits while any one venue and product holds exactly one, so five of its six entries selected a silently empty panel that reads as a broken dashboard rather than as absent data. Which five are dead depends on the selection, which is precisely why filtering on the product as well as the source is load-bearing: bucket size varies by venue — the candle venues write 60s buckets and the daily-only FX vendors write 86400s ones — so a list filtered on the source alone would still offer a value the current selection cannot render. On a cold database this variable is empty, which is the honest signal that nothing has been collected yet, and is strictly better than offering a choice that renders nothing. Allowing it to be empty is what forces the two guards every consumer now carries: the filters compare it as text, and the three analytics panels that also do arithmetic on it wrap it so an empty value becomes null instead. Both exist for the same reason — an empty expansion of a bare numeric reference is a SQL parse error rather than an empty result, and a parse error fails before any row is considered, so casting the filter alone would have left those three panels red on a cold database while the other three read as no data. The sibling ingestion dashboard cites exactly that parse error as its reason for hardcoding the list at all; the trade is taken here deliberately and paid for in both places, rather than reversed silently. It is also excluded from URL sync, unlike the variables above it: a bucket size pinned in a shared or reloaded link can outlive the selection it was valid for and then silently blanks every panel, and since exactly one bucket size exists per venue and product today, there is nothing worth deep-linking. Treat this variable as derived from the other two rather than as state of its own.
list.label: Granularity
list.name: granularity
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT granularity_secs FROM cex_prices WHERE source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND product_id = ${venue_product:sqlstring} ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT i.product_id FROM instruments AS i WHERE ${currency:sqlstring} IN (i.base, i.quote) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM instrument_registry AS r WHERE r.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND r.product_id = i.product_id) ORDER BY 1
list.description: Every pair carrying the selected currency on either leg that the selected venue is registered for. NOT filtered by liveness, deliberately: this picker feeds the panel that discharges the per-symbol acceptance condition, and a liveness filter made that panel show fewer pairs as an outage widened. A pair the venue carries but has not printed lately is marked as quiet in the panel's legend instead of leaving this list.
list.label: Pairs
list.name: pairs
list.query: SELECT i.product_id FROM instruments AS i WHERE ${currency:sqlstring} IN (i.base, i.quote) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM instrument_registry AS r WHERE r.source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND r.product_id = i.product_id) ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT min(bucket_start) * 1000 FROM cex_prices WHERE source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND product_id = ${venue_product:sqlstring} AND granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}
list.description: The epoch-millisecond timestamp of the earliest collected bar for the current selection. Hidden, and not a control: it exists so the All data link can widen the time range to exactly where this series starts rather than to a fixed relative window. A fixed window cannot do that job — collection began on a specific date, so any last-N-days range wide enough to hold every bar also pads the chart with empty space to the left of the first bar, and that padding grows by a day every day. The link deliberately ends at now rather than at the last collected bar, so a series that has stopped still shows the gap between its final bar and the present, which is the only on-chart signal that it is dead. Known soft edge: an aggregate with no grouping returns one null row rather than no rows, so on a selection holding nothing this expands to an empty range bound and the link degrades to resetting the time picker with no indication it did. That is accepted rather than fixed, because the case only arises when there is nothing to show anyway.
list.label: Data start
list.name: data_from
list.query: SELECT min(bucket_start) * 1000 FROM cex_prices WHERE source = ${venue_source:sqlstring} AND product_id = ${venue_product:sqlstring} AND granularity_secs::text = ${granularity:sqlstring}

list.description: Wall clock the hour-of-day profile is expressed in. UTC is neutral and right for comparing across currencies; pick a centre's own zone to read the profile as a local trading day. The weekday/weekend split is always computed on the New York FX week regardless of this setting.
list.label: Hour timezone
list.name: hour_tz

list.description: The coverage table's window, in minutes. Independent of the dashboard time range on purpose: 'what is arriving now' should not change when you pan back to look at history. URL sync is off, like the freshness bound's: a window silently adopted from a shared or stale link fails in the OPEN direction, because a wide window keeps counting buckets for a source that stopped hours ago and so reads as if it were still arriving.
list.label: Coverage window (min)
list.name: coverage_mins

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM spot_ticks ORDER BY 1
list.description: The tick-tier venues: every source that has ever written spot ticks. kraken, erapi, frankfurter, pyth and orca write nothing else, which is why they do not appear under Venue source; coinbase writes both tiers and appears in both. Drives only the Spot ticks panel at the bottom. Multi-select and All by default, because the panel's question is how one product reads across venues; narrow it to isolate one.
list.label: Tick venue
list.name: tick_source
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT source FROM spot_ticks ORDER BY 1

list.definition: SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM spot_ticks WHERE source = ANY (ARRAY[${tick_source:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1
list.description: The product the Spot ticks panel draws, listing only what at least one selected Tick venue has ever printed, so a choice never names a product no selected venue carries. Not time-filtered: a product last printed before the window is listed and draws an empty panel, which is the honest reading of a venue gone quiet. Independent of Currency and Venue product, which are scoped to the candle venue and would otherwise hide tick-only products.
list.label: Tick product
list.name: tick_product
list.query: SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM spot_ticks WHERE source = ANY (ARRAY[${tick_source:sqlstring}]::text[]) ORDER BY 1
